newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Group may top up Creditanstalt bid.
newsitem.headline: Group may top up Creditanstalt bid.

text.p: An international consortium chasing a stake in Austria's Creditanstalt-Bankverein is still intact and may consider putting more money on the table, consortium leader EA-Generali said on Wednesday.
But chief executive Dietrich Karner said EA-Generali would think twice about increasing its involvement in the Austro-German-Italian group.
"As soon as the finance ministry says how it wants to proceed, the members of the consortium will decide whether it makes sense to raise the bid significantly," he told journalists.

"As for EA-Generali...I believe we are already at our limit with our existing five percent stake in Creditanstalt and the additional 1.5 billion schillings ($139.8 million) we are prepared to put up."

The consortium, which includes Germany's Commerzbank and Italy's Banca Commerciale Italiana, had originally bid around 6.7 billion schillings for roughly half the state's 19.9 million Creditanstalt ordinary shares, Karner revealed.
That fell well short of the 18 billion schillings the government had been targetting for its entire 70 percent of voting stock, based on a valuation last year by U.S. investment house J.P. Morgan.
"We did not use the valuation as a starting point. Our bid was based on the share price," Karner said.
At current market prices the government's entire Creditanstalt stake is worth around 13.5 billion schillings.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima rejected the consortium's offer on September 23 and announced he was restarting the sale. A call for bids is expected next week, followed by a four to six-week bidding period.
Karner said there was potential to up the consortium's offer and hinted that there may be less emphasis on a domestic presence in the group.
"If one looks at the individual members there is certainly room to beef up our offer," he said.
"In the past we tried to maintain a balance between the Austrian and foreign members...this was a very important component, but that may not be the case in the next round."

Analysts have suggested the government may have to drop its insistence on an "Austrian solution" to the privatisation of the nation's most traditional bank, given the need for quick revenue from the sale and European Union scrutiny.
"We have to meet not only national conditions but also European ones," Klima conceded earlier this week.
Karner declined to say who might finance a higher bid. Germany's Commerzbank has warned that Austria's price expectations must be "realistic".

He reiterated the hope that Austrian savings bank Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse Bank (First Austrian) would rejoin the consortium. First Austrian opted out on September 6 and later announced it planned a rival bid.
"We are very interested to see an accord with First Austrian. We would welcome their return," Karner said, adding that the two sides were in talks.

He said First Austrian's proposal to set up a holding company with Creditanstalt had faltered on differences over detail. "If we had had a little more time we may have been able to put an agreement together," he said. ($ = 10.73 Austrian Schillings)
